title: Chimps Have Accents, Too - Nautilus
content:
Right now, there’s a quiz bouncing around social media that can pin down where your dialect is from using just 24 questions. Originally developed by Harvard linguists more than 20 years ago, the quiz asks how you pronounce certain words (i.e., merry versus marry) as well as the regional colloquialisms in your vocabulary (hoagie versus grinder versus sub). The result is an eerily accurate map of where your accent comes from, and likely where you grew up. But beyond being a neat party trick, it’s a window into the astonishing diversity of just one language in just one country (the global breadth of English dialects is truly staggering).

Featured Video

But why? 

For starters, they’re strong signals of cultural identity. According to research, our accents actually start in the womb and are so deeply ingrained they even color our non-verbal vocalizations. For example, a 2009 study found that French infants cry with a rising melody, ending on an up note. The cries of German infants, on the other hand, follow a slightly more mournful falling melody. Now, a new study published in PLOS One has uncovered the evolutionary roots of dialects by investigating our closest non-human relatives: chimpanzees.

Read more: “What Became of the Chimps Who Revolutionized Our Understanding of Animal Behavior?”

Like humans, chimps have their own vocalizations used for different purposes (pant-hoots for long-distance communiques, grunts for short-range chatter, etc.), and they also come in different regional dialects. Similarly, these chimp accents signal population identity, but they can change over time. In fact, a 2015 study of two different chimp troops that were translocated together found their grunts eventually blended and converged as the rest of the community did. 

To find out when these distinct accents develop, a team of primatologists studied 30 infant and juvenile chimpanzees, focusing on the acoustic characteristics of their grunts, whimpers, and laughs (the most common sounds produced by young chimps). They found that juvenile chimpanzees produce subtly different vocalizations of all three types, but infants only showed variation in their laughs and grunts (their whimpers were fairly similar). 

In other words, unlike humans, these chimps weren’t born with their accents, they developed them as they matured. According to the team, this is likely because laughter and grunts are more speechlike, while the more constrained whimpers serve as an alarm function, alerting mothers to the location of baby chimps when they’re out of sight. 

But their findings do mirror human vocalizations in another way. Laughter, a non-verbal vocalization associated with positive emotion, actually shows more variation across human languages than negatively tinged vocalizations, like screaming and crying (the French versus German infant study notwithstanding). The same, it seems, is true of chimps. 

Now to find out if they call long sandwiches hoagies or grinders.

title: How Donald Trump Outmaneuvers the Supreme Court
author: @NewYorker
content:
In June, as a federal appeals-court panel considered whether to halt construction of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, Judge Patricia Millett posed a fanciful-sounding hypothetical to the Administration’s lawyer: What if a President bulldozed the Statue of Liberty? “Nothing can be done?” she asked the lawyer Yaakov Roth. “I think that’s right,” Roth replied. Later in the argument, Millett pressed Roth further about his contention that the federal courts have no authority to prevent the construction of the ballroom from going forward. “So this is really something that can’t be stopped in courts—it can only be stopped by Congress,” she said. “I think that’s right,” Roth replied, again. The answer sounded shocking, but it perfectly encapsulated the Administration’s overweening theory of Presidential power—that almost no outside entity has the right to contest its actions in court, and that any challenge that arrives is either too early or too late to change the outcome.

On Monday, a bare majority of the Supreme Court enabled, as it often has, what Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described as Trump’s catch-me-if-you-can approach. In an unsigned ruling, issued through the Court’s emergency docket, five Justices said work on the ballroom could proceed because the plaintiffs challenging the project—the National Trust for Historic Preservation and one of its members, an architectural historian with an interest in the White House—likely would not suffer the kind of “concrete and particularized” injury sufficient to bring a lawsuit. At the same time, the majority said, the Administration would “likely suffer irreparable harm” from a lower court’s order blocking ballroom construction—even though the judge, a George W. Bush appointee, had allowed work to continue on a five-story military complex being constructed beneath the ballroom, in order to protect the President and senior officials. (The Administration has described both the military complex and the ballroom as “vitally required by national security,” though the announcement of the ballroom project, in July, 2025, mentioned nothing about security concerns.)

The majority presented its ruling, which rejected the conclusions of two lower courts, as interim and limited. “Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” it said. But a finding that the project required authorization—in the unlikely event it were to come—would be of little comfort once the ballroom is built. That fait accompli, all ninety thousand square feet of it, is, of course, what Trump has been counting on as his lawyers have fended off court challenges and a two-hundred-and-fifty-person construction crew has raced toward completion. A system premised on legal niceties and compliance with established procedures has proved no match for Trump’s strategy of build first, deal with the consequences later.

The lower courts have, in large part, resisted Trump’s efforts to, as the plaintiffs in the ballroom case put it, “outrun judicial review.” But the Supreme Court’s conservative majority has all too often demonstrated extraordinary deference to the executive branch, while also putting procedural roadblocks in the way of those challenging Trump’s actions. In this case, the majority took a swipe not at the President for overstepping his constitutional bounds but at the district court for daring to interfere with “the activities of a coordinate branch of government.” Courts, it added, “may not exceed the bounds of their lawful authority simply because they may think another branch has exceeded its own.”

Perhaps the most unexpected aspect of Monday’s ruling was that Chief Justice John Roberts dissented. Roberts has typically been supportive of Presidential authority, and reluctant to use the Court’s emergency docket to block the Trump Administration from implementing its initiatives. In the ballroom case, Roberts broke with that stance, not only joining the three liberal Justices but reserving his authority to write the dissent himself. The six-page document did not exactly pulse with fiery rhetoric. “Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers,” Roberts observed, with characteristic mildness. But Roberts did not shy away from his bottom-line conclusion about the ballroom: “That construction is likely unlawful.” Under the Constitution, Roberts noted, Congress has complete authority over the District of Columbia and federal property; it has, he added, “explicitly prohibited” construction on federal property without congressional authorization. “The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds—President’s Park—in the District of Columbia,” Roberts wrote. “Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of it.”

It is not difficult to discern, in Roberts’s words, his frustration with Trump’s behavior: he quoted Theodore Roosevelt on the White House’s “stately simplicity.” There is, Roberts concluded, “reason to ensure that those responsible follow the rules in deciding what to tear down and what to build up at the People’s House.” A rule-follower Trump is not. This does not sit well with the rule-bound Chief Justice.

Roberts’s vote was especially notable because, like other conservatives, he has long endorsed a parsimonious view of the constitutionally based doctrine of standing, which limits courts to deciding actual “cases” or “controversies.” The notion is that only those with a real stake in the dispute, not a generalized grievance, have the right to a hearing. In a 1993 law-review article, while still in private practice, Roberts praised standing requirements as a tool of “judicial self-restraint” that “compels the other branches of government to do a better job in carrying out their responsibilities under the Constitution.” In a 2007 case, in which the Court found that states could seek to force the Environmental Protection Agency to address global warming, Roberts dissented, accusing the majority of engaging in “sleight-of-hand” to find that the states could sue.

On Monday, Roberts turned to the kind of loosey-goosey standing arguments he might once have disdained. “A historic preservationist,” he wrote, “can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.” Jonathan Adler, a law professor at the College of William & Mary who has written on Roberts’s views on standing, told me he was surprised by Roberts’s vote. “The other conservatives viewed this as a case where standing has run amok,” Adler said. (Adler, for his part, said he is inclined to agree.) “Something about this case—the way it was argued, the occupant of the White House, the particulars of what was done to the White House—caused the Chief to see this differently.”

As offensive as the ballroom is, legally and aesthetically, it pales in importance next to other Trump initiatives that are hurtling toward the Court—among them his bid to limit the use of mail-in ballots in time for the midterm elections. Last month, the conservative Justices cleared the way for the Administration to proceed with implementing Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots, which, among other things, ordered the federal government to assemble a list of voting-age citizens in each state and said ballots should be delivered only to eligible voters in special bar-coded envelopes. This move, the order stated, was necessary to “enhance election integrity.” The majority, once again overturning the conclusions of the lower courts, said that a challenge by some two dozen states was premature and that the states lacked standing because they weren’t harmed by the order.

Now a district judge has blocked the regulation adopted by the Postal Service to implement the order. “The record continues to lack any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting,” the U.S. district judge Indira Talwani wrote. “In any event, the USPS’s interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote.” The Administration is appealing, comparing the need to supervise mail-in ballots to the handling of cremated remains. (Ashes, both pet and human, must be shipped in special U.S.P.S.-provided boxes trackable by bar code.) Having mail-in ballots, it argues, “creates an opportunity for the mails themselves to be used to facilitate serious criminal activity—and the Postal Service must have at least as much authority to prevent that sort of harm as it does to ensure that mortal remains are not lost in the mail.”

On Thursday, the Administration returned to the Supreme Court, seeking an emergency order allowing the rule to take effect. With two states poised to begin sending mail-in ballots, the Solicitor General, D. John Sauer, warned, blocking the rule “partially nullifies the Postal Service’s efforts to address the risk that the federal mails will be used to perpetrate voter fraud.” Will the Justices view the matter differently than in their initial ruling? Perhaps—they are now confronting a final rule, with immediate consequences for the midterm elections, and more tangible harm to states. But, even if the Chief Justice were to again defect from the conservative bloc, he would have to lure to his side one of the two other more moderate Justices, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. It is not an auspicious sign that both voted with the majority in the ballroom case.

This Court has been willing, at times, to resist the most egregious of Trump’s excesses; see its decisions this term invalidating his emergency tariffs, rejecting his order eliminating birthright citizenship, and, at least temporarily, frustrating his effort to fire the Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. But, time after time, the majority has acceded to the Administration’s invocation of technical doctrines such as standing to allow policies to remain in place; it has also credulously accepted the Administration’s claims that its actions are necessitated by national-security concerns. The emergency docket has become a mechanism for the Administration to create facts on the ground. The litigation on the ballroom, for example, will limp along, with, almost certainly, little effect on the construction of the ballroom itself. In that sense, the Court’s latest ruling is not strictly about the ballroom. It is, rather, about the judiciary’s willingness to stand up to a President who has repeatedly demonstrated his disrespect for the rule of law. ♦

title: What Happens When a Kid’s Robot Best Friend Dies?
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In this story for MIT Technology Review, Sara Harrison explores the field of social robotics and the growing use of robot companions as therapy for autistic and other neurodivergent kids. These playful machines show promise: Research suggests that they can help children practice social skills and offer something overworked therapists and exhausted parents can’t—a patient companion, available 24/7. But Harrison also reports on their limitations and risks. Does this approach truly work? What about all the data gathered on the child? And what happens when a robot friend suddenly stops working and “dies”? A fascinating and unsettling look at tech that has moved into the most intimate corners of a family’s home.

While Moxie found herself in more and more people’s homes, Embodied still struggled to make money. In 2024, the company announced it would cease operations. Its robots—which depended on external servers that the company could no longer pay for—would descend into a deep slumber. 

Videos of bereft children who seemed to have become deeply attached to the blue bot began to circulate online. “I don’t want her to leave,” wailed one child in a TikTok video. Desperate parents posted on TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit looking for solutions. “My autistic child is devastated and I’m pissed,” wrote one parent. “Hope Embodied gives us a couple days to say goodbye,” wrote another.

title: A Political Operative on the Verge of Self-Deportation
author: @NewYorker
content:
Daysi González, who works to elect Democrats, is gearing up to leave the U.S. as soon as this month. She wants her own party to pay attention.

September 6, 2026

Photographs by Caroline Gutman for The New Yorker

One recent Sunday in August, Daysi González addressed a crowd of about seventy people in a sterile conference room in New York’s financial district. The people who were gathered at tables around her, eating buffet tacos and sipping cans of Coke Zero, were first- and second-generation Americans getting ready to run for office or to work on political campaigns. Some looked younger than thirty and were dressed casually, while others already looked the part of the candidate, in suits or high heels. González, a political consultant who’d come in from D.C., was there to give a seminar on mail—specifically, the postcards that get stuffed into mailboxes every campaign season. “People have to look at it,” González told the group. “Even if it’s just, you know, their mailbox to the recycling bin—they have to look.”

In an age of YouTube ads and paid political-content creators, the notion might seem quaint. But González, who’s thirty-one, has made it her job to figure out how to use the mail to help elect Democrats. On a projected slide deck, she flipped through examples of mailers that she and her firm had worked on: there was the familiar ALEXANDRIA ¡OCASIO! CORTEZ logo, a lotería-themed postcard that read “VOTE FOR OUR COMMUNITY, VOTE FOR RUBEN GALLEGO,” and another one, paid for by the Dolores Huerta Foundation and decorated with Día de los Muertos imagery, that read “VOTA PALOOZA.” González knows the rules of the game, and shared some loopholes that she’s learned along the way—for instance, that political-action committees cannot coördinate with campaigns, but that campaigns can post information, in hard-to-find corners of their websites, about what kind of advertising they happen to need help with. After González concluded her talk, an attendee asked about something she had mentioned earlier—that she was Salvadoran, and living in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status. “I’m so sorry to hear that,” the person said. González, seeming impassive, said, “It’ll work out how it needs to.”

González is one of an estimated two hundred thousand Salvadorans whose legal immigration status is set to expire on September 9th, and one of about a million immigrants in the widening gyre of the Trump Administration’s delegalization drive. For González, who has lived in the U.S. nearly her entire life, the date is a brick wall of a deadline. “That’s when I sell my house, I sell my car, I buy a ticket, I pack everything I own, I get rid of everything I can’t take with me,” she told me.

Unlike most immigrants in America, González has a job that puts her in rooms with powerful people. As a partner at the consulting firm Solidarity Strategies, she tries to help Democrats win some of the most consequential races in the country, including James Talarico’s campaign for Senate, but also smaller names in red districts trying to flip the House. Her biggest client this cycle is the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which has paid her firm more than a hundred and eighty thousand dollars this year, according to the Federal Election Commission. She’s grown friendly with Tony Cárdenas, a client and former congressman from California, who officiated the wedding of her mentor and boss, the political consultant Chuck Rocha. After the seminar, González returned a missed call from Cárdenas, who’d inquired about a New Yorker reporter asking to speak to him. “If you’d be willing to talk to him, there’s nothing I’m really avoiding,” she told Cárdenas in a voice mail. She turned to me: “He probably doesn’t want to say the wrong thing.”

González is introverted, but comes across as warm and cheerful. She smiles while she talks, except when she’s on the verge of tears. Her colleagues at Solidarity Strategies think that she’s good with people, so they’ve put her in charge of dealing with candidates, Party officials, and campaign committees. “Chuck Rocha don’t need to be over there if I’m gonna have a candidate screaming at me and telling me that I’m stupid,” Rocha, the firm’s founder, who appears often, as a straight-talking, cowboy-hatted commentator, on CNN, told me. “That does not go good for Chuck. But Daysi has a way to tell them that they’re stupid, and to do it in such a nice way.”

González has fuzzy memories of El Salvador, which she left at the age of five to come to America. She remembers the day in December, 2000, that her family travelled to San Francisco, on tourist visas, and how her parents dressed her like a señora going to church: cardigan, frilly socks, and her nicest white dress, “to try to look as respectable as possible, I guess,” she said. In the next two months, earthquakes struck El Salvador, and the newly elected President George W. Bush created a legal status for Salvadorans who were then in the U.S. The family eventually settled in Tracy, in California’s Central Valley; many of the kids González grew up around were Mexican and Filipino, so they looked like her. The only thing that set her aside was that her family was Mormon, but her friends didn’t judge. “They were, like, ‘Oh, that’s really random, but good for you,’ ” she said.

Temporary Protected Status gave González the ability to work, but did not qualify her for federal financial aid when applying to college. The Church helped in that regard: González chose Brigham Young University-Idaho, which is heavily subsidized for Mormons. She was there in the lead-up to the 2016 election, and she recalls a professor noticing her Spanish name. “You better hope Trump doesn’t win,” she remembers the professor saying derisively. When González sought legal advice, a lawyer looked her “dead in the eyes” and asked if she had a boyfriend who she could marry for a green card. But she didn’t want her future to depend on one person; she knew of people whose spouses used the threat of deportation to manipulate them. She’d been dating someone for about a month at the time, and broke up with him soon after.

In 2019, González was introduced to Rocha, who had a reputation as a cultivator of Black and brown political talent. Rocha, who is Mexican American, saw something special in González’s immigrant background. “These types of people have had to figure out how to make it through life any way—they could figure out how to make a piece of mail,” he told me. He hired González to help with social media, manage clients, and do administrative work, but, in time, she started designing ads herself. Soon after she joined, the firm was hired to help run Bernie Sanders’s 2020 Presidential campaign, which meant that González was the only person handling the rest of the clients at the firm’s K Street office; she became an equity partner within a few years.

After that election, as she built her life in a capital governed by Democrats, González grew alienated from her church. “It was jarring to be living here, going through the immigration struggles that I’m going through, and then, like, high-ranking leaders in the Church are MAGA. Why am I associating myself with this?” And she began to worry about her status again in 2024, as the second Trump Presidency came into view. After Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee for President, the polling looked bleak enough that González sat Rocha down to talk, anxious that she’d have to leave the country.

The life that González had made in America over twenty-five years—the college degree and the career, the house in northern Virginia she owns with her sister, the Honda HR-V she paid off last year—was possible because the question of her status had settled into a cycle of unstable predictability. New Presidents continued to find that conditions in El Salvador merited the extension of the “temporary” status, and she dutifully paid the fees and filled out the paperwork every eighteen months. (By itself, T.P.S. doesn’t provide a path to a green card or citizenship.) Trump attempted to cancel the status during his first term, but the courts had ruled it unlawful; after he won again, Joe Biden, during his last week in office, approved another eighteen-month reprieve. González had never got this close to zero before. This past Monday, less than two weeks before the extension was set to expire, she packed up some belongings she’d kept at her office: three pairs of high heels, a pair of fuzzy slippers, a tube of toothpaste. “Having to take some stuff out of my desk—like, I never got that far, other times.”

Washington consultants are hired to solve problems—of variable legality and morality, depending on the client, but problems nonetheless. There is always a fix that no one else has thought of, a loophole to be discovered. This has been, more or less, Rocha’s approach in trying to help González stay in the States. He began making calls to the White House shortly after Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election, to lobby for the T.P.S. extension—“Look, I’ve worked for Big Joe,” he recalls saying—and has connected González with lawyers and advocates. But González understood the system better than all those people. She’d tried her chances at the work-visa lottery system, but was unsuccessful; she looked into a relative sponsoring her, but that would take years. Knowing that there was nothing they could do, she told Rocha to stop.

Rocha said that he would, but he didn’t; he just stopped telling her about it. As recently as last month, he said, he had talked privately with people who worked in Trump’s White House. “Send me her stuff,” one staffer said, “but also know that this can cut both ways if I raise this too high.” Rocha has many friends in Washington, but his attempts to change González’s situation have left him feeling powerless. “You mean I can’t call a senator? I can’t call the chairman of the Hispanic Caucus and just fix this shit?” he said, raising his arms incredulously. “No matter how many important people you know, no matter how much money you think you have, that you’ve made at this little firm—none of that matters.” He grew agitated thinking of Obama’s decision not to pursue immigration reform when he had legislative majorities. “Now me and my team are paying for that,” he said, before quickly adding, “nothing against Barack Obama.”

Rocha wishes that the elected officials his firm has worked for would give speeches from the House floor to emphasize that the people ensnared by Trump’s policies are not criminals. But Democrats have become more tentative to speak on immigration since the Obama years. Andrea Flores, who worked in the Obama Administration and served as a border official under Biden, told me that Biden lacked interest in pushing legislation to regularize the status of longtime residents. The House Minority Leader, Hakeem Jeffries, she pointed out, didn’t even mention immigration in a recent press conference announcing an agenda of Democratic priorities should they retake the majority. “There may not be an immediate electoral gain in prioritizing immigration,” Flores said, “but there is an absolute electoral risk and loss by allowing the system to be as dysfunctional as it is, and allowing the Republican Party to continue to weaponize that dysfunction against Democrats.”

Rafael Collazo, the executive director at UnidosUS Action Fund, a Latino civil-rights advocacy group and a client of González’s, told me that her case should underscore a “failure of leadership” in D.C. that “we’re all responsible for.” “But,” he added, “in particular, Congress, and, in particular, the people that claim to be more progressive on immigration issues—the Democratic Party, Democrats in Congress—they haven’t done enough. None of them have done enough.”

González is planning to go back to El Salvador—a place where she has few relatives left, and where, although Rocha has offered to keep her as a remote worker, she’s not sure she’ll be able to keep her job. Then she’ll try to immigrate to another country, such as Spain. (Spain offers a digital-nomad visa, with a fast-tracked path to citizenship for Latin American nationals—“Like a sort of reparations program,” she said.) She’d started documenting her final month of T.P.S. on Instagram, initially hoping to catch the attention of someone in government, but she now thinks of the videos as more like “diaries.” In one, she notices that she’s out of rice, and laughingly considers whether she should bother buying another bag.

On work calls, González told me, there’s now a preamble: “ ‘I’m so sorry you’re going through this, like, let me know if you need anything. But when is that mail going to drop? Have you had the chance to get the invoice out?” And even though she works to elect Democrats, González said that the candidates whom she helps elect may have little to say about her case. “I don’t know what more they could add, other than like, ‘Damn, that sucks,” she said, before putting on a politician voice: “And that’s why I want to win and fight for immigrants.” Cárdenas, when reached by phone, said something along those lines: “Should Democrats do more? Yes, and the opportunity to do more is really going to be in their hands when they control the House, when they control the Senate, when they control the Presidency.” While in Congress, Cárdenas helped González navigate her immigration status and the attendant anguish that came with it. He left after twelve years in 2025, feeling like he could’ve done more—but, then again, he added, “I worked my butt off, man . . . and you only have so much staff.”

How would you spend your last days in America? For González, the natural answer involves BTS concerts. She’s become a superfan since Trump was reëlected, and has found community in the fandom. On Friday, she boarded an early flight to Los Angeles to attend the final show in the North American leg of the K-pop group’s world tour. She had gone to the band’s concert in Baltimore about a month earlier, and got home at four in the morning. “As the concert was ending, people around me were probably, like, ‘Oh, she’s crying because the show’s over, she’s a diehard fan,’ ” she recounted. That was part of it, but also, “I knew that I was going back to this mess, and that the countdown’s started, right?” Her favorite BTS song is “00:00 (Zero O’Clock),” a melancholy anthem about uncertainty, and starting over. ♦

title: Your Boss Is Watching You - Nautilus
content:
This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine.

Featured Video

Ready for a Whopper with a side of Orwell? Earlier this year, Burger King announced the rollout of Patty, an AI chatbot imbedded in headsets that tracks if cashiers neglect to say please and thank you and chimes in when a soda fountain is running low.

Advances in AI, cameras, sensors and tracking software have given employers unprecedented power to monitor employees. They now observe the physical location of workers, the length and content of phone calls, keystrokes per minute, and even the tone and pitch of conversations with customers.

Now, as companies search for new ways to watch their workforce, researchers are taking a close look at the consequences of constant surveillance.

Employee monitoring has become standard practice in multiple industries and workplaces. Drivers delivering packages or pizzas are increasingly being watched by AI-powered surveillance systems. Many employees in Amazon warehouses are continuously tracked through handheld scanners, badge swipes and workstation software.

Technologies that keep tabs on employees hold a strong appeal for corporate leadership, says Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany. Leaders may believe that close surveillance can help identify top performers, increase efficiency or improve safety, he says.

In practice, though, such benefits are elusive. When König reviewed studies on employee monitoring in the 2025 issue of the Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, he found little to suggest that electronic surveillance improved performance. “My general take is that [monitoring] isn’t going to matter as much as employers assume,” he says.

Despite the lack of evidence, the global market for employee-monitoring technology is expected to exceed $4 billion in 2026, largely due to major companies in North America. A New York Times investigation in 2022 found that eight out of the 10 largest private US employers, including United Parcel Service, Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, tracked productivity metrics of individual workers, often in real time.

US postal workers are also closely watched. Delivering mail “feels less like public service and more like working inside a quiet surveillance state,” said a Reddit user in 2025. “We’re tracked down to the second. Every scan. Every step. Every stop. They monitor our GPS in real time. They can pull up on us unannounced. We get questioned for things as human as needing the restroom or checking a package twice.”

Any employer of any size can get into the monitoring business. Amazon Web Services sells thousands and thousands of software programs for employee monitoring, says Michele Molè, an employment law researcher at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. Adding a monitoring app to the workplace can be as easy as downloading Spotify, he says. But instead of music, employers get a stream of data about how each employee is behaving every minute of their day.

Companies that hope to increase their workforce’s performance through monitoring face a basic obstacle in human nature, König says. Workers might briefly up their game, but they tend to revert to their normal routines. “They become habituated,” he says. In his review, he pointed to growing evidence that even body cameras worn by police — an especially high-profile, high-stakes example of surveillance — don’t significantly change the behavior of either the police or the public over the long term.

When workers do respond to monitoring, there can be unintended consequences. A 2020 study found that electronically monitored truck drivers were less likely to exceed daily limits for driving hours, but they also were more likely to crash.

König is far from the only skeptic. “There’s really very little evidence that the mere implementation of monitoring employees is, in itself, going to increase productivity or performance,” says Daniel Ravid, a management researcher at the University of New Mexico.

Ravid conducted a 2022 meta-analysis that combined the results of studies involving more than 23,000 subjects in laboratory experiments and workplace settings, including workers in call centers and offices and police on patrol. Taken together, the studies found no correlation between levels of monitoring and employee performance.

That’s partly because some employees find workarounds to monitoring, even if that means tapping their keyboard periodically while they’re reading a book at lunch. “People are incredibly creative and adaptable, and they’ll find ways to reassert their freedom when it’s threatened or taken away,” Ravid says.

Ravid’s meta-analysis found that any type of monitoring — subtle or obvious, incidental or invasive — tended to increase workplace stress. “I think anything that undermines a sense of dignity is also going to undermine employee attitudes,” he says.

A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada underscored the potential downsides of monitoring: Employees who perceived that they were being surveilled on the job reported that they felt more pressure and stress and less autonomy and privacy at work.

In an age of “datafication,” it’s not surprising that companies would look for new metrics to evaluate employees, says Kirstie Ball, a management researcher at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “The systematic gathering of data about people and what they’re doing is part and parcel of modernity,” she says. “Surveillance becomes a means of getting things done.”

But not every company knows how to make good use of all those data points, Ball says. “There are many pitfalls along the way. Are you measuring what you think you’re measuring? Are you interpreting the data correctly according to the purpose that you gathered it, or are you looking at it just because you can?”

Employee surveillance without any coherent plan to use the data has become a commonplace scenario in modern companies, König says. Many workplaces end up collecting data simply because they have the technology, not because surveillance supports the company’s overall business strategy. “They end up with terabytes of data on a drive somewhere but don’t know what to do with it.”

Modern surveillance is an inherently electronic exercise, but companies can’t just install an app and expect results, Ravid says. “If managers think that they have a perfect way to measure performance because they have advanced technologies, they’re wrong,” he says. “They still need human insight and conversations to contextualize that data.”

Laws protecting employees from overly invasive surveillance generally haven’t kept pace with technology, says Molè, who wrote the 2026 book Monitored at Work. While the European Union has strong employee privacy laws, with additional legal protections in nations like Italy, Spain, France and Germany, workers in the US have far fewer safeguards and are more likely to be placed under a microscope.

In 2023, three current or former Amazon delivery drivers in Colorado filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon claiming that they were under excessive AI-assisted surveillance and that delivery quotas made it difficult to take necessary breaks. “The drivers were forced to pee in bottles,” Molè says. “This is not happening in Europe.” Amazon called for arbitration, noting that drivers work directly for outside delivery service providers who have contracts with the multitrillion-dollar company, not Amazon itself. The case is ongoing.

Other legal issues can lurk in the fine print that comes with monitoring software. Bosses who download monitoring apps they can’t customize are essentially letting outside companies take control of their employees’ data with little oversight or knowledge of how the data could be used. “We need more labor laws that target providers of technologies,” Molè says. Surveillance companies should be required to work directly with companies and their employees to clearly explain the technologies and tailor each product to meet specific needs and reach specific goals, he says.

Theoretically, monitoring could be a part of a healthy company culture that encourages success, Molè says. “People under monitoring should have a sense of being valued, and the monitoring should be truly meaningful for improving everyone’s working conditions and methods,” he says. “Good monitoring is based on mutual trust.” Companies that thoughtfully build their own system for tracking employee outputs instead of superimposing some “creepy and odd” tool found online are more likely to see actual benefits, he adds.

Success is certainly possible. Headbands that track brainwaves may seem invasive, but an Australian mining company found that such technology helped reduce fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. A 2024 study of remote workers on Upwork found that the productivity of top-performing workers dropped nearly 20 percent after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software without explanation, suggesting that the software had some benefits.

But productivity didn’t fall when that high-performing group was told they had the opportunity to go without supervision because of their impressive output, underscoring the importance of good management — leading the researchers to conclude that spending money on good managers could yield better results than spending it on monitoring software.

Transparency can go a long way to improving workplace culture, Ravid says. His meta-analysis found that, compared with workers who are surveilled without much explanation or consent, workers who have a clear understanding of how they are being monitored and how the data will be used also have a greater sense of fairness and job satisfaction.

New technologies will continue to join the ranks of Burger King’s Patty and other monitoring devices in the modern workforce. But if companies don’t change their basic approach, the results will likely be the be the same: suspicion and confusion for employees and few tangible benefits for employers.

This article originally appeared in Knowable Magazine, a nonprofit publication dedicated to making scientific knowledge accessible to all. Sign up for Knowable Magazine’s newsletter.

title: Why We Like Things
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
“Taste is a new core skill,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman declared earlier this year—one voice in a growing chorus of pronouncements about the centrality of judgment and preference in an economy built on artificial intelligence. And yet taste itself is largely undefined by many of its loudest proponents. Celine Nguyen considers the historic relationship between automation and taste; the “seemingly irrelevant, unimportant” inputs that shape our critical perceptions; and the perils of wielding taste like a cudgel. A striking, insightful blend of criticism and personal essay.

Today’s frontier models are trained on enormous quantities of data. One takeaway from Anthropic’s 2025 settlement with a group of authors, in which the company agreed to pay $1.5 billion (or an estimated $3,000 per book) for scraping copyrighted books from shadow libraries like LibGen, is that its models have “read” at least 482,460 books. But even Claude Opus 4.8 hasn’t written a short story that I enjoy more than those by Lydia Davis or Jessi Jezewska Stevens — both of whom, despite being prodigiously well-read, have almost certainly read fewer books.

Fascinating (in our humble opinions) stories about criticism and taste

A Portrait of the Artist as an Amazon Reviewer

Oscar Schwartz | The New Yorker | November 27, 2024 | 2,629 words

“Between 2003 and 2019, Kevin Killian published almost twenty-four hundred reviews on the site. Can they be considered literature?”

Everybody Gets a Star

Jaya Saxena | Eater | July 18, 2024 | 3,114 words

“Twenty years after its debut, Yelp has changed how we think about reviewing everything and anything.”

A Notorious Pitchfork Reviewer Was My Biggest Musical Influence

Dan McQuade | Defector | January 31, 2024 | 2,944 words

“Pitchfork reviews have always been just as much about where and how music fits in the culture as they have been about the music itself.”

title: The Blood of Dawnwalker sold 1 million copies in just 3 days
author: Ted Litchfield
content:
On September 5, Rebel Wolves took to Twitter on the official Blood of Dawnwalker account to announce that the dark vampire RPG had already surpassed one million copies sold just three days after its September 2 launch. "Thank you for playing, sharing, supporting, and being part of the community," the developer wrote in its celebratory post.

I was in a Star Wars Zero Company-shaped hole during Dawnwalker's contemporaneous review period, but everyone on our team who played has been pretty pleased with this very Witcher-like RPG from ex-Witcher devs. Australian editor Shaun Prescott awarded it an 83% in his review, praising the storytelling and combat, but wishing that Rebel Wolves had gone harder on Dawnwalker's unique time mechanics.

"Blood of Dawnwalker is an effective piece of worldbuilding and storytelling then, but it doesn't make good on its promise as an innovative piece of RPG design," Shaun wrote. "Maybe Rebel Wolves worried that too many players would fall afoul of the passage of time and thus loosened its severity."

He was even more on the money than he could have realized when he wrote that: Some of the first mods for Dawnwalker do away with the time limit entirely. I appreciate the "have it your way" ethos mods can have, but I think a bit of friction can be a very good thing. I unilaterally declare PC Gamer to be a pro-time limits publication.

Zooming out, it's exciting to see both Dawnwalker and Zero Company get rave reviews and strong sales during this challenging time for the industry. Disney hasn't announced any numbers for Zero Company, but it's sitting at a beefy 15,562 reviews and "Very Positive" on Steam a week and a half after launch, a compelling indicator that it's doing well. The similarly multi-platform Blood of Dawnwalker, by comparison, is at 8,296 total reviews after having passed the million mark in total sales.

Of course, Zero Company's success has a tinge of uncertainty to it that Rebel Wolves has been spared: 80% of developer Bit Reactor's staff is reportedly on furlough, awaiting sales revenue and further investment to secure their jobs.

Ted has been thinking about PC games and bothering anyone who would listen with his thoughts on them ever since he booted up his sister's copy of Neverwinter Nights on the family computer. He is obsessed with all things CRPG and CRPG-adjacent, but has also covered esports, modding, and rare game collecting. When he's not playing or writing about games, you can find Ted lifting weights on his back porch. You can follow Ted on Bluesky.

title: All the RPS Supporter rewards for August 2026: fatty felines, GTA 6 pondering, and a heap of barely washed radishes
author: James Archer
content:
It’s been an unusual month

You there. Have you completed the RPS Supporters survey? You don’t even need to be a Supporter. In fact, it’s better for certain questions if you aren’t. Either way, this is your chance to play a part in making sure our subscription rewards are as rewarding as rewards can be, which some might say is a reward in itself.

Less abstractly, Premium Supporters also get to read cool words like these: all the exclusive articles we posted in the month Of August. And yes, I did decide to start listing them chronologically.

RPS Supporter rewards for August 2026

Scout Report: Cato colon Buttered Cat makes a gentle puzzling challenge of an old bit

Sin Vega investigates how much game juice can be squeezed out of a piece of toast yoked to a cat. The answer: enough for a decent puzzle-platformer, appaz.

Very well, I'll show you my desk, but there's nothing you can say about the mouse mat that I haven't already grumbled to myself

Powerless to resist Julian’s obvious baiting, I continue this series of RPS staff desk tours. I’ve sinced added a Sherma figurine to my collection of Small Characters, though, so beware that the whole thing is already out of date.

I never developed a taste for Soulslike games and it's my old boss's fault

The heartbreaking tale of how our Editorial Director never got gud.

I'll make you a deal. You can see my desk, but only if you make a sacrificial offering to Ugly Squidward

Another desk tour – and our most in-depth to date – courtesy of infuriatingly youthful guides guru Callum.

Sin returns to appreciate the silly side of satirically charged, lowercase-c cyberpunk point ‘n’ click Neofeud 2.

A few days prior to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Netflix thing, Julian ponders the practical considerations around covering (probably) the biggest game of the decade when it isn’t actually a PC game. Cheers to everyone who commented their thoughts on this!

Modding up Skyrim for the first time in years has convinced me I might have been too quick to scoff at Bethesda themselves adding fishing to it

Mark eats his words, and/or trout, while modding himself an angling career in Skyrim. Fish fear him.

Booth snacks of Gamescom 2026, reviewed

Speaking of eating, I drew on my culinary expertise by assessing the finger food available at last week’s Gamescom, which at one point even included – get this – some vegetables.

See you in September! Oh, shit.

title: 1666: Amsterdam is buggy and sometimes bewildering, but there's real ambition too
author: @eurogamer
content:
There's an old Sam Raimi profile in the New Yorker I think about quite a bit. This is because, mid-way through the piece, Raimi says one of the most interesting things I've ever heard a film-maker, or any kind of creative person, put into words.

Raimi's talking about the films he made with his friends when they were really young. Super-8 stuff. The camera would swoop in on two toy soldiers stood up on the carpet, and then the film would cut to Sam and a friend standing next to each other. And this is the thing: nobody watching the film would understand what the two shots cut together were meant to represent. They were telling you that Sam and his friend were the soldiers on the carpet. That's what you were meant to take away. But everybody in the audience missed it.

Raimi then explains - and I wish I had the quote - that as a kid he was making films that were so bad that nobody could even tell they were bad. The audience was just bemused. For the audience to understand that they were watching a bad film, Raimi would first have to become a better film-maker.

I appreciate this sounds like a brutal way to open a discussion of a video game, but be warned: if anything, I suspect I like 1666: Amsterdam a lot more than most people will. Even so, there's no ducking the fact that it is an odd game. And it's often odd through necessity, I imagine.

And this is why I thought of Raimi. In one sequence early on in the game - no matter why any of this was happening - I was wandering through a 1990s boutique hotel in Amsterdam almost entirely naked. I was trying to get to an outside space that I had just seen in a vision. But my path was blocked, and it was blocked by strange, low-res groupings of people, their faces not much more than bland cartoons. They were standing together, perfectly still if my memory is correct, clustered in doorways. What to make of it all? These groupings, so almost-sketched in, each one with at least one entirely replicated person amongst their number. And so still! So blank of expression. I had no idea what to think. Was this a dream? Were these people possessed? Had we fallen outside of time and space somehow?

What I now reckon is this: the game needed to hem me in, to drive me towards tackling a specific puzzle about getting to that outdoor space. And it wanted me to tackle that specific puzzle in a specific way. So it used crowds to close out doors I wasn't meant to go through. But because of the challenges of making an ambitious game with a relatively small team and a limited budget, it had to rely on low-res character models. And it had to duplicate some of them. And I don't think it could animate them at this specific point. That's my guess.

Image credit: Panache Digital Games

This led to Raimi-style confusion. Forget good or bad, what even is this? What am I meant to take from this moment? But untangling this whole sequence also led me to understanding something about 1666: Amsterdam. I'm on its side. It's not bad. In fact, some of it is really good in principle. But in trying to execute on an ambitious plan, the whole thing's over-stretched itself. And hence a game about witchcraft contains accidental surrealism along with the real thing.

This is the pact you make with 1666: Amsterdam, I think. To enjoy it you have to survive a bunch of things that are not really that enjoyable. There's the AI stuff in the game, of course, which is just as miserable as always. Then there are the bugs and rough edges. Alongside the odd crash, I've had to quit and restart numerous times because the cat I was playing as - I'll get to this - descended into the game's geometry and got stuck. Walking through Amsterdam's busy streets, the people I pass are animated, but they're still regularly duplicated, a city of twins and triplets. And I cannot work out the rules governing who has collision turned off (most people) and who doesn't (some people, some times).

A lot of voices online are saying that the game's in too rough a shape to be heading to early access like this. And I guess that's true. But I guess what's also true is that, again, a fairly small team is making this game, and the design is complex and at times pretty audacious. Sometimes, I imagine you need to get money coming in just so that you can keep on trucking. There you are: another kind of pact.

Anyway. As I write this I'm still in the early sections of 1666: Amsterdam's current early access build. I'm told there's about 15 hours in it total, and I'm just nearing the end of the first proper mission. I'm about six hours in. The reason I've stopped playing now to write this is because I've hit a bit of a milestone. I've just beaten a boss, sure, and I'm about to get to the outer arm of what I assume the main loop is. But more than that, after being intrigued and frustrated and confused by what I've been playing, I've finally hit on what feels like the peculiar magic of this game. I've found the thing that makes it worth playing and that actually makes it kind of wonderful.

1666: Amsterdam is a tale of witchcraft and devilry, and it's made by Patrice Désilets' team at Panache. Panache made the memorably odd and frustrating and thought-provoking Ancestors, in which you guide an early hominid through the wonky chicanes of evolution. But Désilets himself is probably best known for his work on Assassin's Creed.

And 1666: Amsterdam initially looks a lot like Assassin's Creed. This is potentially a problem, because that's a really bad lens through which to view this game. But again, you play someone in the present who's learning about someone in the past. You dance between time periods - three in this game: the present day, the 1990s, and the year 1666. In the 1666 part you play someone in a hood that hides all but the surly curl of their lip, and that person is tasked with tracking down various targets in the city and getting rid of them. That sure sounds like Assassin's Creed!

But in fact things are very different. I'm going to focus on the 1666 part here because, from what I can tell, it's both the main event and the most satisfying part. Noa, who you play as in this era, is a kind of assassin, perhaps, but she's primarily a witch. And while she can gad about the waterways when nobody's looking, and engage in staff-based combat when she really has to, she can't mantle and wall-run like Ezio and all the rest of them. For the most part she has to keep her witch self concealed and move about Amsterdam meekly, avoiding any kind of scrutiny.

So rather than scaling towers and dropping out of the sky to put a blade through someone's throat, she wanders the streets and listens to crowd chatter and slowly works out the identity of her next witchy target. In the first proper mission, this is a prosecutor of some kind who is known for being particularly tough on witches. With her perp IDd, Noa then needs to gather a bunch of evidence before the prosecutor can be unmasked and dispatched - cue boss fight.

Real talk: I am not enjoying combat in this game. With its jumps and flourishes it looks wonderful, but Noa is too delicate - a few hits and she's gone - and her dash move is too useful for creating space. Together, these things mean that I avoid the more complicated options I have, which involve special attacks and witch-based triggering of environmental hazards, and I just lamp people with my wooden stick and then dash out of harm's way. It gets me through most battles without too much annoyance, but it is the opposite of fun. For me, I think the diagnosis is this: failing is so arduous that I just want to work through the fights as conservatively as I can. In other words, the balance is off.

But the stuff in between that? This is the part of the game I think I may love. And this really is an inversion of Assassin's Creed. Rather than a huge city to scramble over the outside of, 1666: Amsterdam gives you a single neighborhood of Amsterdam at any one time, but it seems to model the insides as well as the outsides of most buildings. It's practically an immersive sim, albeit one that feels like it's arrived at that genre unintentionally. This is that rare open world game where you can actually step through most doors and see what's lying beyond them. All of this is delivered with wonderful lighting that invokes the spooky art of the Dutch Golden Age.

This sounds overwhelming: a whole neighborhood to explore. In truth, the game's pretty quick to put you onto the correct target. Within minutes of leaving the house to uncover my foe, I had been directed towards a trial taking place and I was pretty sure I had my man.

Now I had to prove it, though. And that meant finding out where this prosecutor lived and then infiltrating their house to look for the things I needed to prove their demonic guilt. And so I discovered that a lot of 1666: Amsterdam is about sneaking through someone's private residence and trying to open as many of its locked doors as you can.

The house I wanted into was both extremely large, being spread over several floors, and heavily patrolled by guards. Going in there as Noa was not an option. Instead, I could use my witch's cat. This cat is where the game's parkour-like elements come in. It can climb up gutters and jump between ledges. And because it's a cat in a city filled with rats and other vermin, it can pretty much go wherever it wants. Pretty soon I had got the cat into the house I was targeting and I was casing the joint, threading through guards' feet, locating the kitchen, the dining room, various bedrooms.

Image credit: Panache Digital Games

But vital rooms were still locked off. And at this point the game really becomes a spatial puzzle. Over time I realised I could leave the house via an upstairs window and move around the outside ledges a little to access some of the locked rooms, at which point my cat could unlock doors from the inside. Neat trick.

Even neater, I could possess specific guards - any that were visibly scared by the presence of a cat - and then use them to walk about the building and access new parts of it. Certain possessed guards could club other guards and get them out of the way. And one of them, I found, could actually invite Noa inside, taking me along with me, as it were, and then Noa could explore spaces and root through drawers and get the evidence she (I?) needed.

Now. This is very complex, and it's also a bit silly. A lot of big moments in the game are signalled by a stately Dutch person having a massive scrap with a cat. But what I like about all this is not just that it's a bunch of lovely illicit spatial challenges - who doesn't like nosing through other people's things in a game? What I like is that it seems to get at an interesting truth about the era that the game examines.

I'm not an expert on the art of the Dutch Golden Age, but I am a fan. And even if you're a very lapsed fan, you'll experience this game as a bunch of pleasant little instances of shocked recognition. The game opens with a collection of still lives, the paintings of everyday objects and fruits and vegetables that a master like Adriaen Coorte could really make sing. His bunches of asparagus look as vast and godly as alien space ships. His apples and pears look like dwarf planets floating undiscovered in the Kuiper Belt.

And then you're in Amsterdam itself. The complex windows. The red brick. The little arches and doorways. You only need to see a handful of Vermeers or Rembrandts to know how lovingly this stuff has been observed. I walked 1666: Amsterdam and I was in a permanent flashback for a life I had never lived, but had only experienced through oil paintings.

But here's the thing. My limited understanding of one of the real breakthroughs of Dutch art is that this prosperous country - prosperous for some deeply awful reasons, obviously - was one of the first to really turn art inwards. People like Vermeer stayed in their houses for the most part and just painted what they found there.

These are great artists of material culture, and they spoke to a time of merchants and traders. They spoke to a time where your home and its contents were clues to the puzzle of who you truly were - or who you wanted to present yourself as, at the very least. (This goes back a few centuries to van Eyck, incidentally. And van Eyck, to use a bit of art history jargon, is the absolute freakin' business. When the zombie apocalypse finally comes, you'll find me in the National Gallery trying to ease his Arnolfini Portrait out of an open window.)

Marry this art to a game about poking through other peoples' houses and there's something there that I think is really harmonious. And there is something about Panache, too. This company makes audacious, overly ambitious games that don't entirely work but also won't leave my head at the very least. I didn't love playing Ancestors, but I still think of it quite regularly when one of its ideas strikes me as being intriguing or under-explored elsewhere.

And similarly I was in the Wallace Collection last week when a friend and I stumbled across Pieter de Hooch's A Boy Bringing Bread. We were both captivated by this scene, which uses a series of rectangles to recreate the interior of a Dutch household where a child has come to the door and is being greeted by a woman. Inside the house you sense a cool, spare elegance. A nearby chair has a cushion on it, and art hangs from the walls. But out through the door you can see a stretch of tiling, an arch, and another house across the street, where another figure, perhaps the boy's mother, is waiting for him.

It's one of those paintings that opens out the past and encourages you to imagine what it would be like to step onto its streets. And in 1666: Amsterdam, you can kind of do that.

A copy of 1666: Amsterdam was provided by Panache Digital Games.

title: Less than a week after launch, The Blood of Dawnwalker developer is already getting to work on the sequel
author: Andy Chalk
content:
With more than one million copies sold just a few days after its release, a "very positive" rating on Steama, and an enviable 83% review score from PC Gamer, vampiric horror RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker is a hit. And less than one week after its debut, developer Rebel Wolves is already planning what comes next.

Unsurprisingly, "what comes next" is more Dawnwalker: Jakub Szamałek, narrative director at developer Rebel Wolves, wrote on LinkedIn (via Dexerto) that "we're not resting on our laurels," but are already thinking about where to take the game from here.

"I'm looking for a lead writer to help me and the narrative team craft the next chapter in the Dawnwalker saga," Szamałek wrote. "We're looking for someone who, to put it bluntly, writes EXCEPTIONALLY well, has a track record of excellence and experience in team management."

The job listing provides more detail about what's involved and it's heavy stuff, with responsibilities ranging from writing in-game documents and dialog to collaborating with the narrative director—that's Szamałek—and other team leads, and managing the entire writers team. You'll also need "a minimum of six years of experience as a writer/narrative designer in the video game industry with a track record of outstanding achievement."

That might sound like a lot for a studio that's only got one game under its belt, but remember that Rebel Wolves was founded by veterans of CD Projekt: Szamałek himself was principal writer on Cyberpunk 2077, Thronebreaker, and the standalone release of Gwent, and before that earned writing credits on The Witcher 3 and its expansions. In fact, numerous CD Projekt personnel took time last week to offer congratulations on the game's launch.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.
